idiom_name: ParseRule table of function pointers with a parsePrecedence loop (clox style)
implementation_notes: C has no closures, so the parselet set becomes a table of function pointers indexed by token type - struct ParseRule { ParseFn prefix; ParseFn infix; Precedence precedence; } - exactly as the clox compiler builds it. Handlers receive the parser context explicitly (or read a file-static parser struct), and parsePrecedence(min) calls the prefix handler for the current token, then loops while the next token's precedence is at least min, invoking the infix handler with the left operand. Precedence is an enum whose numeric order defines binding, and the table must cover every token type because the loop indexes it unconditionally. This is the lowest-level realization and is hand-written by construction; when the grammar outgrows expressions, a yacc/bison grammar is the usual alternative, and the Crafting Interpreters chapter recommends staying with the table precisely because it keeps the parser small.
pitfalls: The table is indexed by token type with no bounds check: when the TokenType enum grows and the designated-initializer table is not updated, the parser reads a stale or zero-initialized rule instead of failing loudly.
Precedence values must be strictly ordered and complete; a duplicated or inverted value silently changes grouping (a - b - c) with no diagnostic anywhere.
Recursion depth follows expression nesting and chain length: unbounded input overflows the C stack, so a depth counter with a clean error is required wherever input is not fully trusted.
